name: Kings Corners
description: Kings Corners is a social, Solitaire-like card game played by 2 to 4 players. Unlike competitive trick-taking games, it focuses on building sequences of alternating colors onto a central cross-shaped layout. The goal is to be the first to empty your hand. It is widely considered one of the best family games for all ages due to its simple rules and visual layout.

history.origins: Dates to the early 20th century in America. It evolved as a communal version of standard Solitaire (Klondike), enabling multiple people to play on a shared board.
timeline: 1920s: Gathers popularity as a parlor game.
1950s: Becomes a standard family card game in the US.
Present: A staple for teaching children basic card sequencing and colors.
history.cultural: Known for being a low-stress, social game that bridges the gap between Solitaire and competitive play.
history.evolution: The 'Corner' rule (where Kings must be played and then built upon) is the game's defining mechanic, differentiating it from simple 'Go Fish' or 'Slap' games.

setup.players: Two to four players. The game is said to be good for four players. A standard 52-card pack is used; the first dealer is chosen at random and the turn to deal passes clockwise after each hand.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Aces are low (sequencing on Kings is King-Queen-Jack...2). No, wait. Standard Kings Corners Ranking: K-Q-J-10-9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2-A.
setup.dealing: Each player is dealt 7 cards. Four cards are placed face-up in a cross (the 'T' or '+' shape). The rest form the draw pile.

rules.objective: Be the first player to play all cards from your hand onto the table piles.
rules.gameplay:
1. Players take turns. Each turn begins with drawing 1 card from the stock.
2. You can play any card from your hand onto a pile if it is one rank lower and a different color (e.g., a Red 7 onto a Black 8).
3. You can move an entire pile onto another pile if the bottom card of the first fits on the top card of the second.
4. **Kings**: If you have a King, it *must* be played into one of the empty 'Corner' slots (diagonals of the cross). Once there, it forms a new foundation pile.
5. Empty Slots: If one of the original 4 foundation slots becomes empty, you can place any card (or sequence) there.
keyRules: Kings must go to corner slots
Can move entire piles onto other piles

strategy.basic: Prioritize emptying the 4 main slots by moving sequences. Every empty slot is a massive opportunity to play cards that don't fit elsewhere.
strategy.intermediate: The 'King Save': If you already have cards that fit on a King, wait for an opponent to play their King into a corner first so you don't have to waste your turn filling a corner slot.
strategy.advanced: Sequence Consolidation: Always look for ways to merge existing table piles. This frees up the 4 main slots, which can then be filled with any card, potentially dumping a large part of your hand at once.
tips: Don't build too deep on the 4 main piles if you have a King; you want the Corners to be most accessible.
Watch your opponents' colors. If they are primarily drawing Red cards, try to play Black cards to the board to entice them to 'tack' their cards onto yours.
